metadata.title: Can We Decarbonize the Construction Industry?
metadata.audience: students: smart people getting started with AI

beats.narration_text: Imagine two buildings. Same number of floors, same purpose, same structural strength. They look almost identical. But one has a much lower carbon footprint. How? The answer might be hidden in what they're made of, and how they were built.

show.event: carbon bars: one long, one short

beats.narration_text: Construction is one of the most resource and carbon intensive industries. Steel, cement, concrete, glass, transportation, heavy machinery and construction waste all add to its emissions.

show.event: seven emission sources land as named

qc.sparse_reason: build-up beat: seven emission sources land one per word

beats.narration_text: And unlike the electricity a building uses, many of these emissions are released before the building even opens. This is called embodied carbon.

show.event: materials → construction → opening day → years of use
brace + 'embodied carbon' over the first two

qc.sparse_reason: build-up beat: timeline first, embodied-carbon ring and label land at the second sentence

beats.narration_text: Take concrete. Its key ingredient, cement, is made by heating raw materials to very high temperatures, often with fossil fuels. And the chemistry itself releases carbon dioxide. When limestone is heated, it breaks down into lime. This step is called calcination.

Steel has its own carbon heavy path, especially when it's made with fossil fuel intensive processes. So decarbonizing construction isn't just about using less energy on site. It's about material science, structural engineering, chemistry, logistics and lifecycle assessment.

qc.sparse_reason: build-up beat: materials, then the reframe, then five disciplines land one per phrase

beats.narration_text: Can we use less material without compromising safety? Can we swap in lower carbon materials? Can we design parts to be reused instead of demolished?
This is where AI could make a difference. AI assisted design tools can compare structural options side by side, weighing material quantities, cost, strength and embodied carbon.

show.event: options A B C table with bars (illustrative)

beats.narration_text: Computer vision can track materials on site, to spot waste or chances for reuse. And predictive systems can improve equipment scheduling, logistics and energy use.

show.event: camera view with detection boxes: reuse / waste

qc.sparse_reason: build-up beat: vision panel first, scheduling panel lands at the second sentence

beats.narration_text: And machine learning can give early carbon estimates, so teams make lower carbon choices before designs are locked in. The key is making carbon a design constraint from the very beginning, not an afterthought.

show.event: room-to-cut-carbon curve falls over the project

qc.sparse_reason: build-up beat: curve and markers first, constraints land at the last sentence

beats.narration_text: Because the lowest carbon material isn't always the newest one. Sometimes the best climate decision is using less material, reusing what already exists, or making a building last longer.

qc.sparse_reason: build-up beat: framing line first, three options land one per phrase

beats.narration_text: So here's the question: If we could calculate the carbon footprint of every design decision before construction begins, would carbon become as important as cost and structural safety?
